chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from Harun ibn Muslim from Mas'adah ibn Sadah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him saying:

"Everything that is yours is permissible until you know for certain that it is forbidden, so you leave it on your own accord. This is like a garment that is on you which you have bought, but it is stolen property; or a slave in your possession, perhaps he is free and has sold himself, or was deceived and sold, or was compelled; or a woman under your marriage, and she is your sister or your milk-sister. All matters are upon this principle until something else becomes clear to you, or evidence is established regarding it."
ai.seo_question: What is the default ruling for possessions and transactions in Shia jurisprudence until proven otherwise?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) articulates the foundational Shia legal principle of *al-asl fi al-ashya' al-halal* (initial permissibility), asserting that possession implies validity until specific evidence of defect—such as theft, hidden slavery, or kinship—emerges. This hadith, cited in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* under leases, underscores the burden of proof lying on the claimant of invalidity, reflecting the juristic preference for stability in transactions and property rights. It highlights the practical application of *istishab* (presumption of continuity) in daily commercial and familial interactions.
